name: Pwo Karen of Huay-Hom-Nok village, Mae Tha district, Lamphun
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

catalog_quote: [p.46] In Pwo Karen, a phonological word has only one main (strong) stress. The stress is placed on the last syllable of a phonological word. That is, a strong stressed syllable shows the end of a phonological word. Thus a phonological word in this study may be called a stress group as well. ... The syllabic pattern of Pwo Karen is basically monosyllabic. There are also a small number of disyllabic words and an even rarer number of trisyllabic words. [p.65] Stress is defined in terms of intensity (volume) and duration of (vowel) length. It functions in syllable rank. In Pwo Karen, stress is predictable by the types of syllables and its position in phonological word. Therefore, the word stress needs not to be marked overtly at the phonemic level. [p.67] The nuclear syllable is a major syllable and always takes strong (primary) stress. It always occupies the last position in the word. [p.69] Stress is predictable by the syllable position in the phonological word and by the syllable structure: the final syllable in a phonological word is the major syllable, the non-final syllable in /Cə/ structure is the presyllable, and the non-final syllable in a phonological word is the minor syllable. Therefore, stress needs not to be marked in the phonemic transcription.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word (stress-group) stress is fixed on the final syllable: every phonological word ends in a 'major' syllable (full C(C)V + tone) which carries the single strong/primary stress; non-final full syllables ('minor syllables') carry weak stress and non-final Cə presyllables (neutralised mid pitch, no tone contrast) carry none. Stress is predictable and not phonemic. Cooke, Hudspith & Morris 1976 (Hot district; PL C-43 pp.190, 205) independently describe the same system as weak stress on preposed /ə/ syllables vs normal stress on all others, plus an obligatory phrase/sentence stress on a normal syllable whose examples all fall word/phrase-finally (ɣaŋkhu' 'earth', ɣaŋkhukhu' 'upon the earth', kəchaŋ' 'elephant', kəchaŋphu' 'elephant calf'); Phillips 2017 p.24 calls it 'an iambic stress pattern in disyllables, in which the initial syllable is reduced'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Chuensukon p.66: 'Weak Stress (Secondary Stress).. occurs on any minor syllable' i.e. every non-final full-vowel, tone-bearing syllable of a di/trisyllabic word carries weak stress (marked [ˌ]); Cə presyllables have zero stress. Cooke et al. 1976 distinguish only weak (preposed) vs normal stress at word level.
new_statements.exceptions: None to the final-syllable rule; presyllables/minor syllables can never be word-final (Chuensukon p.68 'Every peripheral syllable can occur in any position, except the final one'; Cooke et al. p.190 preposed syllables 'never occur utterance final'; Phillips & Tucker 2021 minor syllables 'never occur alone or word-finally'). Chuensukon p.46 hedges only for monosyllables: 'The strong stress usually occurs on that syllable.' Cooke et al. p.207 note certain normal-syllable morphemes optionally reduce to preposed (unstressed) syllables in non-final position (e.g. /bɛ/ 'manner' > /bə/).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word = 'stress group' (Chuensukon), the unit of the intonation group; mostly mono- and disyllables, rare trisyllables; examples are citation forms from a 1,117-item wordlist. Cooke et al. additionally posit a phrase/sentence stress superimposed on one normal syllable per utterance (extra loudness and duration), shown on the last syllable of words and phrases in their examples. Language is tonal (5 tones Chuensukon; 4 tones + glottalised variants Cooke et al; 6 tones Phillips); stress is non-contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement (Chuensukon 1995) describes the Pwo Karen of Huay-Hom-Nok village, Tambon Tha-Mae-Lob, Mae Tha district, Lamphun province, which Glottolog files under pwon1235 (Northern Pwo). The corroborating published description, Cooke, Hudspith & Morris 1976, describes 'Phlong', the plains subdialect of Hot (Hod) district, Chiang Mai, which Phillips 2017 explicitly calls 'the Hod variety of N. Pwo'; Phillips 2017 and Phillips & Tucker 2021 describe Northern Pwo Karen generally (Omkoi/Hod area, Chiang Mai). None of these is Eastern/West-Central Thailand Pwo (pwoe1235) or Phrae Pwo (phra1234). Note that Chuensukon's ch. 2 literature review (thesis pp. 44-45) summarises her own 1993 study of a Sangkhlaburi (West-Central = Eastern Pwo) variety; the quoted chapters 3-4 are the Lamphun (Northern Pwo) analysis.

sources.note: sec 3.1: 'N. Pwo is an isolating language with major and minor syllables. Major syllables (C(C)VT) are stressed and make use of the full inventory of consonants, vowels, and tone. In contrast, minor syllables (Cə) are reduced and never occur alone or word-finally. They have a limited single initial consonant inventory and unstressed /ə/ as the only vowel, with no tone.' Instrumental study of VOT etc., not of stress.
sources.venue: Context effects on the acoustic realization of stops and affricates in Northern Pwo Karen

sources.note: sec 1.3 (p.8): syllables are either reduced minor syllables (/ə/ nucleus, no tone) or major syllables with full inventory and one of six tones. p.24-25: 'Phonologically, N. Pwo, like other MSEA languages, features an iambic stress pattern in disyllables, in which the initial syllable is reduced.' p.70: proclitic tʰə= 'reduced to proclitic status with no stress or tone'. Refers to Cooke et al. 1976 (Hod variety) and Phillips 2009 (Omkoi variety) for phonology.
